Recent research supports treating sampled ranking as a distinct evaluation condition. RecSys 2025’s [On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) examines resolution, fidelity to full ranking, robustness, and recovery of ground-truth model rankings; candidate sampling can change model ordering. [Subbiah et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06371) demonstrate benefits from correcting sampled rank estimates for WARP/LambdaRank training. These findings justify auxiliary sampling-sensitivity checks, but do not establish that corrected metrics improve this benchmark’s pinned HR@10.

[Distributionally-Informed Recommender System Evaluation (2024)](https://841.io/doc/disteval.html) argues for examining utility distributions and sources of uncertainty beyond aggregate point estimates. Practical calibration proposal: bootstrap users within each category, preserve paired outcomes across model variants, and recompute the equally weighted four-category macro HR@10 difference. Report category intervals and the macro interval. With only four fixed categories, category-resampling uncertainty should be exploratory; user bootstrap intervals also exclude training-seed variability and adaptive-search selection bias.

For diagnostic predictive validity, use chronological holdouts drawn exclusively from training histories. Across controlled architecture/loss/sampling variants, test whether probe changes predict held-out HR@10 changes; reserve variants for assessing generalization and report rank correlation, improvement-direction accuracy, and uncertainty. Compare identical checkpoints under repeated uniform-negative draws, popularity-based candidates, and full-catalog ranking on these auxiliary holdouts. Keep the host’s validation users, 99 unique negatives, seed, and selection metric unchanged. This is a proposed experimental framework, not a validated diagnostic recipe from the cited papers; score margins alone do not demonstrate intervention validity.
